newsitem.title: CHINA: Gold price fall could turn into rout.
newsitem.headline: Gold price fall could turn into rout.

text.p: Gold's slide to 12-year lows in New York on Thursday, on news Australia's central bank had sold a large chunk of its reserves, could turn into a rout if producers are panicked into selling, traders said on Friday.
"I think we could see a big wave of selling from producers," said Dick Gazmararian, executive vice president of Republic National Bank's Asia Pacific precious metals operations.
Raymond Chan Fat-chu, president of Hong Kong's Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society concurred and said investors could follow the producers down and offload their gold holdings.
"If gold prices come down further, there could be a crisis of further dishoarding from people who are holding back. Then the lack of confidence could bring a chain-like action."

Spot gold closed at $325.00/50 an ounce in New York on Thursday after briefly falling to $323.70, its lowest since early December 1985 when gold was recovering from a nadir of $281 set in February 1985.
In Asia trade on Friday, Hong Kong midday gold opened firmer on shortcovering, but by 0430 GMT had dropped to $324.70/325.20 an ounce in two-way trade, dealers said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia announced early on Friday it had sold 167 tonnes of its gold reserves in the past six months.
The weak price trend could continue as central banks' attitudes towards gold have changed with far more lucrative reserve assets available to them, dealers said.

One London-based analyst estimated that holding gold in their reserves costs central banks worldwide $15 billion a year in lost income when compared with returns from investing in other interest-bearing assets.
"It's a trend and will continue over the next few years until one central bank steps in to buy, because it's very much a herd mentality," one senior Hong Kong dealer said.

Chan said the market uncertainty and lower prices could persist through the summer until at least September when he expected prices would stabilise and central bank sales become The European Union (EU)'s monetary committee, comprising national treasury and central bank officials will meet in September in Luxembourg to discuss European monetary union and the use of the banks' reserves including gold.
The gold price flop was not all bad, sources said.
A market shakeout below $300 per ounce may in fact be good for the market by renewing investor interest and reviving an upside potential, Gazmararian said.
Chan agreed, noting that lower prices, if they didn't collapse completely and destroy confidence, could boost gold consumption in Asia.

"This year Hong Kong will break a record (in gold imports). When gold prices come down, gold floods here and is redistributed to neighboring countries. It's cheap gold, and Asia is trying to beat the record again," he said.
